title: Arbëresh: The Albanian Diaspora that Preserved a Medieval Language | Wikitongues Fellows #2
description:
To prevent language extinction, Wikitongues invests in language activists, accelerates endangered language revitalization, and defends multilingualism worldwide.

Wikitongues Fellows are saving their languages and keeping their cultures alive. We started the fellowship in 2021 to support the leaders of new language revitalization projects with micro-funding, training, and volunteer support.

Martin Di Maggio is a second generation British speaker of Arbëresh, being the only member of his generation, whom he knows of, born in the diaspora who can speak the language fluently. Arbëresh is an Indo-European, Albanian language with an estimated 100,000 speakers. However, the exact number is unclear: although Arbëresh is a part of the Albanian language family, a majority of Arbëresh live in Italy, where the national census does not collect data on minoritized languages.

title: Lucy speaking Igbo | Igboid | Nigeria | Wikitongues
description:
Igbo is the principal native language of the Igbo people, an ethnicity in the Southeastern part of Nigeria. Igbo languages are spoken by a total of 31 million people. The number of Igboid languages depends on how one classifies a language versus a dialect, so there could be around 35 different Igbo languages. The core Igbo cluster, or Igbo proper, is generally thought to be one language but there is limited mutual intelligibility between the different groupings (north, west, south, and east). A standard literary language termed 'Igbo izugbe' (meaning "general igbo") was generically developed and later adopted around 1972, with its core foundation based on the Orlu (Isu dialects), Anambra (Awkadialects), and Umuahia (Ohuhu dialects), omitting the nasalization and aspiration of those varieties.

title: Maryori and Odilia speaking Kaqchikel | Quichean | Mayan languages | Wikitongues
description:
The Kaqchikel language (in modern orthography; formerly also spelled Cakchiquel or Cachiquel) is an Indigenous Mesoamerican language and a member of the Quichean–Mamean branch of the Mayan languages family. It is spoken by the Indigenous Kaqchikel people in central Guatemala. While languages of the Mayan family are not mutually intelligible, Kaqchikel is closest to the Kʼicheʼ (Quiché) and Tzʼutujil languages. Kaqchikel is taught in public schools through Guatemala's intercultural bilingual education programs.

title: Suhyar speaking Mandailing | Austronesian | Batak | Wikitongues
description:
Mandailing, or Batak Mandailing, is an Austronesian language spoken by the Mandailing people in Sumatra, the northern island of Indonesia. Mandailing has a rich literary tradition dating back centuries and has traditionally been written in the Batak script, an abugida in which each symbol represents a vowel-consonant combination (though today, the Latin script is predominantly used). Despite a speaking population of roughly 1.1 million, the language has been classified by Ethnologue as “endangered” on account of the dominance of Indonesian as the major language of government and education and in the region.

title: Marco speaking Friulian | Romance | Rhaeto-Romance | Wikitongues
description:
Fiulian, natively known as Furlan or Marilenghe (“mother tongue”), is a Romance language spoken in the Friuli region of northwest Italy. It is closely related to other “Rhaetian” languages like Romansh, spoken in southeast Switzerland, and Ladin, spoken in the Dolomite Mountains of northern Italy. Friulian has a long history of literature dating back to at least the 13th century. Today, Friulian is spoken by around 600,000 speakers. Although it is officially recognized and protected by the Italian government as a minority language, however, the language is considered “definitely endangered” by UNESCO.

title: Elie speaking Jidi (Judeo-Shirazi) | Judeo-Iranian | Languages of the Jewish Diaspora | Wikitongues
description:
Judeo-Shirazi, or Jidi, is an Judeo-Iranian language traditionally spoken by the Persian Jewish community living in and around the Iranian city of Shiraz. Judeo-Shirazi preserves many older forms of Persian and has a rich and storied literary tradition. During the late-20th century, many within the Jewish Shirazi community emigrated to the United States, particularly to New York City where around 4,000 individuals reside today. With only around 200 elderly speakers, Judeo-Shirazi is considered “moribound.” However, efforts are currently underway to document this language. 

The speaker interviewed in this video is Dr. Elie Alyeshmerni, who was born in Shiraz and now resides in Los Angeles, California. This interview was conducted via Zoom by Haideh Herbert-Aynehchi, and transcribed and translated in English by Noah Khaloo, with the HUC-JIR Jewish Language Project, which you can learn more about here: https://huc.edu/schools-programs/institutes-centers-projects/jewish-language-project/

title: Gerard and Patrick speaking Occitan | Romance | Langues d'Óc | Wikitongues
description:
Occitan, referred to as lenga d’óc by native speakers, is a Romance language spoken in southern France, Monaco, and in regions of Catalonia and Italy. The term Occitan originates from the Occitan word for “yes” — óc — which derives from the Latin word hoc meaning “this.” All six of the major dialects of Occitan are considered severely or definitely endangered by UNESCO, due in part to policies that prohibited the use of minority languages in schools in the early twentieth-century. Recently, however, there has been widespread support for programs aimed at revitalizing Occitan through the development of bilingual signage and immersion education.

Recorded in Annonay, France.

title: Timilehin speaking Nigerian Pidgin | West African Pidgin English | English Creole | Wikitongues
description:
Nigerian Pidgin, also referred to as Pidgin or Naijá, is an English-based creole variety spoken primarily in Nigeria. Nigerian Pidgin emerged from the various waves of European contact during the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade and has since developed into a lingua franca among the many ethnically and linguistically diverse communities of Nigeria. Like most creole languages, Naijá exists on a continuum of features that can differ based on region and speaking context. While Nigerian Pidgin English is not recognized as an official language of Nigeria, it is one of the most widely spoken languages in the country with over 120 million speakers.

title: Phillip speaking Soga (Lusoga) | Bantu | Niger-Congo | Wikitongues
description:
Soga, or Lusoga, is a Bantu language spoken in Busoga regions of eastern Uganda. With around 3 million speakers, Lusoga is one of the most commonly spoken languages in Uganda alongside Luganda, English, and Swahili. For decades, English has been the primary language of education in this region, but efforts are currently underway to integrate Lusoga language curriculum and educational materials into Busoga schools.

title: Adalberto speaking San Juan Del Rio Zapotec | Valley Zapotec | Otomanguean | Wikitongues
description:
San Juan Del Río Zapotec is a Zapotec language primarily spoken in the Valles Centrales Region of Oaxaca, Mexico. It is a dialect of Western Tlacolula Valley Zapotec spoken by the indigenous peoples of Oaxaca in southern Mexico and by many migrant communities across the United States. However, despite its name, Valley Zapotec is not mutually intelligible to the over 50 Zapotec languages spoken in the region. With around 28,000 speakers, Valley Zapotec is currently classified as “stable” by Ethnologue.
